events.title: Gandhi Begins the Salt March
events.description: Mohandas K. Gandhi set out from Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad with 78 followers on a roughly 240-mile march to Dandi on the Arabian Sea coast to protest the British salt tax and monopoly. The march grew as it progressed, and Gandhi broke the salt law by making salt at Dandi on April 6.
events.significance: The Salt March became a landmark act of nonviolent civil disobedience, galvanizing the Indian independence movement and drawing worldwide attention to British colonial rule.

events.title: Anschluss: German Troops Enter Austria
events.description: German forces crossed the border into Austria, following pressure from Hitler on Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg, who had resigned the previous day. Austria was annexed into Nazi Germany, and the annexation was formally proclaimed the following day.
events.significance: The Anschluss was a key step in Nazi expansion before World War II, violating the Treaty of Versailles and demonstrating the unwillingness of Britain and France to confront German aggression.

events.title: Girl Scouts Founded in the United States
events.description: Juliette Gordon Low organized the first Girl Guides troop meeting in Savannah, Georgia, with 18 girls. The organization was renamed Girl Scouts of the USA in 1913.
events.significance: The organization grew into one of the largest youth organizations for girls in the world, promoting leadership, outdoor skills, and civic engagement.

events.title: Tim Berners-Lee Proposes the World Wide Web
events.description: While working at CERN, British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee submitted a proposal for an information management system using hypertext to link documents across a network. His supervisor described it as 'vague but exciting.'
events.significance: This proposal laid the foundation for the World Wide Web, which transformed communication, commerce, and access to information globally.

events.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt Gives First Fireside Chat
events.description: Days after taking office, President Roosevelt delivered the first of his radio addresses to the American public, explaining the banking crisis and the reasons for the bank holiday in plain language.
events.significance: The fireside chats pioneered the use of mass media by presidents to communicate directly with citizens and helped restore public confidence in the banking system during the Great Depression.
